tools.model: Osler · Sackett · Snow   (+ Darwin in research preview)
tools.modelFamily: OpenEvidence Model Family (Osler / Sackett / Snow / Darwin) — proprietary, base architecture never disclosed
tools.notes: OpenEvidence released a named model family on 2026-09-03: Osler (fast, default, ~5s), Sackett (deeper search, ~30s), Snow (successor to Deep Consult, ~5 min), plus Darwin (frontier reasoning model, research preview and API by application only). All three production models are user-selectable via a model selector in the interface and free for verified clinicians. The stack is custom domain-specialized LLMs trained on licensed peer-reviewed literature (NEJM, JAMA specialty journals, NCCN, Springer Nature) and deliberately not on the open internet, trained and served on Baseten (Baseten Training + Baseten Embeddings Inference; end-to-end latency 700ms to 160ms; 'billions of custom, fine-tuned LLM calls per week'), with a corpus-anchored retrieval layer that selects the most relevant papers and grades evidence strength (EvidenceGrade, GRADE-inspired). Frontend is Next.js on Vercel; backend is Python/ML. No base model, parameter count, or architecture is disclosed for any of the four models; CEO Daniel Nadler describes an 'ensemble architecture' of roughly half a dozen smaller specialized models (retrieval, ranking, synthesis) rather than one large model. Separately, Reuters reported on 2026-09-22 that Anthropic's technology provides back-end support for the free, locally adapted OpenEvidence rollout across ~100 low- and middle-income countries — the only public sign that any part of OpenEvidence runs on Claude.
tools.conflict: Baseten says OpenEvidence trains 'custom open-source models' but never names a base model, so 'fine-tuned open-weight base' is inference, not disclosure. The Sep 3 announcement is product naming, not a technical spec. The Anthropic link is back-end technology for the free LMIC rollout only — no evidence the US product's answers are Claude-generated. A third-party systems-design essay speculates on H100 sizing and LoRA adapters; plausible, but unverified, so not treated as fact.

stack.v: Licensed journals, NCCN, Cochrane — not the open internet
Ensemble of ~6 specialised models (retrieval, ranking, synthesis)

tools.model: GPT-6   (Sol at Instant–Extra High; Pro = Astra)
tools.modelFamily: GPT-6 (GPT-6 Sol at Instant-Extra High; GPT-6 Pro powered by GPT-6 Astra at Pro effort)
tools.notes: Free, NPI-verified U.S. clinician workspace (MD/DO, NP, PA, pharmacist) sitting alongside the user's normal ChatGPT workspace in the account switcher. OpenAI's own product page now advertises 'Higher limits on GPT-6 - our most capable model for healthcare', so the launch model GPT-5.4 has been superseded. In Chat, GPT-6 is GPT-6 Sol (Instant, Medium, High, Extra High) and Pro effort is GPT-6 Pro powered by GPT-6 Astra; per OpenAI's health lead (Sept 10, 2026) verified U.S. clinicians get free GPT-6 Astra (Pro) access through ChatGPT for Clinicians. The Epic chart plugin is enterprise-only; image generation is unsupported; content is never used for training. No published clinician-specific model-picker doc was found, though Astra/Pro availability implies at least effort-level selection.

tools.modelFamily: Doximity post-trained reasoning model (open-weights base, trained and served on Fireworks AI)
tools.notes: Doximity does not run a named third-party frontier model here: it post-trains its own clinical reasoning model on open weights with Fireworks AI and serves it in-house. Ask has two inference modes that the clinician can pick from a single dropdown - Instant (fast) and Thinking (deeper, shows its work) - with automatic Instant-to-Thinking escalation for complex questions; the mode list is the closest thing to a user-selectable model choice. Stack is RAG over a physician-governed evidence library (millions of peer-reviewed publications and specialty-society guidelines refreshed daily), a fixed registry of deterministic clinical calculators/drug lookups, a structured medical knowledge graph for exact doses and interactions, and a bibliography service that resolves DOI/PMID/authors so citation metadata is never generated from model memory. PeerCheck physician review (12,000+ physicians) closes the loop as training signal. Key contrast with Doximity Scribe: Ask runs Doximity's own post-trained model, while Scribe's note summarization is OpenAI GPT-4o with OpenAI transcription under a Doximity-OpenAI BAA; since 2026-09-14 Ask is embedded inside Scribe as its copilot. Ask also now carries UpToDate content alongside its own answers (Oct 2026).
tools.conflict: Doximity's engineering article names no base model family, only 'a post-trained reasoning model', and Fireworks — its training partner — says it 'trains open models' without naming the base. Third-party trackers name bases Doximity has never confirmed. The version number is firmer: the Bedside Bench leaderboard (Nov 6, 2026) lists Doximity Ask V7, and a Doximity VP states V7 was developed and evaluated with it. Resolved to V7, with the base model recorded as undisclosed.

tools.modelFamily: OpenAI models via Wolters Kluwer's FAB platform (model-agnostic; also selects models on Microsoft Foundry)
tools.notes: Wolters Kluwer never names a specific model behind UpToDate Expert AI. What is disclosed: the June 2026 expansion of the OpenAI enterprise collaboration states that UpToDate Expert AI was rebuilt 'by working closely with OpenAI' and that 'moving to the latest models' significantly increased clinical relevance, with OpenAI APIs and platform capabilities deployed inside Wolters Kluwer's own model-agnostic enablement platform, FAB (grounding, tracing, logging, tuning, evaluation); the same company's Ignite 2025 case study says UpToDate Expert AI is 'enabled by Microsoft Foundry's secure model access', i.e. multi-model selection across OpenAI/Anthropic/Google on Azure. What users get instead of a model picker are subscription tiers - UpToDate ($579/yr), UpToDate Pro Plus ($699/yr) and Trainee ($219/yr) all ship the same Expert AI feature set; Pro Plus adds CME state-tagged topics, Kidney Dosing, antidepressant switching and MobileComplete, and a new UpToDate Pro Premium bundle adds Lexidrug Premium. No user-facing model selection exists. Grounding is closed to the open web: answers surface only peer-reviewed UpToDate content with inline topic citations, visible assumptions and rationale, plus Lexidrug dosing; CME credit accrues inside the AI workflow; a Clinical AI Validation Framework (1,669 queries / 15,000+ criteria) reports 99.9% clinical alignment.
tools.conflict: Wolters Kluwer never names a specific GPT version for UpToDate Expert AI — 'the latest models' is the actual published claim — so this records OpenAI models without pinning a version rather than inferring one. Earlier (2023-2024) Wolters Kluwer described a bespoke LLM 'exclusively trained on UpToDate trusted content'; both can be true over time, but the current base model is not stated. Note the site previously recorded 'GPT-5' for this tool in benchmark contexts; those were the benchmark's comparison models, not UpToDate's production stack.

tools.modelFamily: Mixed: OpenAI GPT-5.x frontier + Abridge in-house + NVIDIA Nemotron-derived
tools.notes: Abridge explicitly runs a multi-model stack and refuses to name one model: frontier models for high-value reasoning plus purpose-built in-house models for ASR, per-section note generation and ICD-10 coding. Their most recent tech-blog post (Oct 2026) describes an LLM-based clinical ASR model (audio encoder + projector + LLM backbone, SFT then GSPO reinforcement learning) that beats Whisper-large-v3, Qwen3-ASR-1.7B, GPT-4o, GPT-Realtime-2, Gemini 3.1 Pro and Gemini 3.5 Flash on WER and medical-term miss rate; the base LLM is not named. On Jun 11 2026 Abridge and NVIDIA announced a first-of-its-kind foundation model for clinical conversations built on the NVIDIA Nemotron open model family, trained on Blackwell with pre-/mid-/post-training on de-identified data, exclusive to Abridge's platform and expected later in 2026. Model selection is explicitly not exposed to the customer — 'selecting and orchestrating the right model for each task is our responsibility' — and model changes are communicated through a partner release-update process. Clinical decision support is grounded with a curated evidence library (UpToDate, NEJM, JAMA, Wolters Kluwer, ADA, AAFP, Neurology, JCO) with citations, integrated with Epic, Oracle Health and athenahealth.
tools.conflict: Abridge uses different models per task: the nursing blog (May 2026) names GPT-5.4, the CDS/note-generation blog (Apr 2026) names GPT-5.5, and CEO Shiv Rao said in April 2026 that ~70-80% of what Abridge does is driven by in-house models with ~30% involving a frontier model. Resolved to GPT-5.5 as the most recently named frontier model.

tools.notes: Ambience says its platform is 'powered by proprietary AI reasoning models', and for point-of-care CDI and Chart Chat it names OpenAI explicitly — built on 'OpenAI GPT-5's advanced reasoning capabilities with Ambience's proprietary models', with the coding model trained using OpenAI's Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (the ICD-10 model that beat board-certified physicians by a 27% relative margin). Ambience has deliberately moved up the stack from models to infrastructure: Ambience Chorus (announced Aug 2026) is the shared AI infrastructure and agent harness — a System of Context maintaining a source-linked understanding of the patient across the longitudinal chart, plus a System of Action. No user-selectable model — 'Ambience Standard' prices on outcomes rather than tokens or seats. Cloud/SaaS via the Microsoft Azure Marketplace since Apr 2025, with Epic, Oracle Health/Cerner and athenahealth integrations; no vendor statement of on-premises deployment. Chart Chat is grounded in BMJ Best Practice with citations.

tools.notes: Nabla has deliberately stopped naming frontier models: its Sep 2026 explainer states it combines proprietary and commercial models, each selected for the performance it brings to a specific step of clinical documentation, and that Nabla trains its own smaller specialised models for precise documentation tasks in French and English rather than one big model. The help centre confirms notes are generated 'using a combination of in-house natural language algorithms and Large Language Model (LLMs)'. The only model lineage Nabla has named publicly is the speech layer: 'our model is based on Whisper', fine-tuned on 7,000 hours of manually annotated medical encounter audio, with added hallucination suppression and medical-term accuracy. Integrity is enforced by an atomic-fact verification pass — every note is split into atomic facts checked back against the transcript and patient context before the note is written. A trust-centre AI Model Card (CHAI version 3, Apr 2026) is available only on request, so the underlying models are not public. Nabla hosts on Google Cloud (US for US clients, Belgium/EU otherwise) with speech-to-text via Microsoft Azure, and holds an exclusive partnership with AMI (Yann LeCun's world-model company) for future agentic, FDA-certifiable systems. No user-selectable model; clinicians choose note templates, custom instructions and a personal medical dictionary instead.

The one named LLM is Claude, and only for Heidi Evidence (launched Feb 2026), 'in part built on Claude, Anthropic's AI models', grounding answers in HealthPathways, EMGuidance, MIMS, Vidal, NICE and BMJ Group content with citations. What is verifiable: Dragon Copilot (launched 2025-03-03) merges Dragon Medical One dictation/ASR with DAX Copilot ambient listening plus fine-tuned generative AI with healthcare-adapted safeguards; the note generator is a 'trusted core medical model, fine-tuned on millions of real-world patient encounters' and then specialty-adapted (clinician's primary specialty selects which note model runs). An Azure engineering post describes a 'signals loop': they fine-tune on a clinical-data repository and re-evaluate whenever new foundation models ship, with current models ~50% better than the base foundation model - i.e. the base is a moving target that Microsoft has not named. ASR is now Microsoft in-house: MAI-Transcribe-1.5 replaced the prior transcription model in Dragon Copilot's multilingual workflow across 58 languages (July 2026). Content filtering uses Azure OpenAI Service classifiers, and the Information Assist extension is powered by Microsoft Azure Healthcare Agent Service doing RAG over admin-enabled vetted sources (FDA, CDC, MedlinePlus, MSD Manuals, DailyMed, plus customer sources) with a Clinical Safeguards engine and inline reference numbers. Lineage: the older Nuance DAX Express was explicitly built on OpenAI GPT-4 hosted in Azure OpenAI. Clinicians do not pick a model; they pick their specialty, their templates, their Information Assist sources, and partner-built Marketplace apps/agents.
tools.conflict: Older coverage (2023-2025) states the generative layer is GPT-4/GPT-4o on Azure OpenAI; current Microsoft documentation names no model and describes an in-house fine-tuned core medical model plus MAI models for speech. The in-house description is the current one, so no GPT claim is recorded for 2026.

tools.modelFamily: Apple Foundation Models, 3rd generation (built in collaboration with Google)
tools.notes: Apple's Health app is explicitly 'built with Apple Intelligence at its core'; Apple has not published a per-feature mapping from AFM 3 models to individual Health features, so the model stack is disclosed at family level. The current generation (June 2026) is AFM 3: two on-device models (AFM 3 Core, a ~3B-parameter dense model, and AFM 3 Core Advanced, a 20B-parameter sparse model activating 1–4B parameters) and three server models on Private Cloud Compute (AFM 3 Cloud workhorse, AFM 3 Cloud Pro for agentic tool use and complex reasoning, and ADM 3 Cloud for images). AFM 3 Cloud Pro runs on NVIDIA GPUs in Google Cloud while keeping Apple's privacy guarantees. Separate from the AFM text models, Apple's at-home movement evaluations (flexibility, strength, balance, VO2 max) run entirely on device using vision-based AI models, and newer Watch sensing uses purpose-built ML models. Server-side AFM 3 Cloud usage is subject to daily limits, and Apple says paid expansion of server-model access is planned.

tools.modelFamily: MedGemma (Gemma 3 backbone + SigLIP medical vision encoder); family also includes MedGemma 1 4B multimodal, 27B text-only, 27B multimodal
tools.notes: The latest MedGemma is MedGemma 1.5 4B, released 2026-01-13 as the only 1.5 variant (4B multimodal instruction-tuned, google/medgemma-1.5-4b-it). It is built on Gemma 3 (decoder-only transformer) with a SigLIP image encoder pre-trained on de-identified medical images, and adds CT/MRI volume interpretation, whole-slide histopathology, longitudinal chest X-ray comparison, bounding-box anatomical localization, lab-report extraction and text-EHR understanding over MedGemma 1 4B. Weights are open (Hugging Face + Vertex AI Model Garden) under the Health AI Developer Foundations licence, run on a single GPU via transformers/vLLM or a custom serving container, and are explicitly positioned as 'starting points for developers to evaluate and adapt' — so MedGemma is a developer foundation, not a shipped Google clinical product. Google's own health AI runs on Gemini (Personal Health LLM is 'a version of the Gemini model fine-tuned for health'; AMIE is a research system), while MedGemma/TxGemma are the open-weight developer line. Model choice is the developer's: pick 4B vs 27B, multimodal vs text-only, pre-trained vs instruction-tuned, then fine-tune; Google requires validation for any use case.
tools.conflict: Documentation lags the release: the HAI-DEF page lists MedGemma 1.5 as 4B multimodal only, while the Hugging Face collection and GitHub README still describe only the MedGemma 1 lineup — the 27B variants were never refreshed to 1.5. There is no MedGemma 2, and the wider Gemma family has moved on (Gemma 4) without a medical refresh, so MedGemma remains a Gemma 3 derivative.

tools.notes: Claude for Healthcare (announced 2026-01-11) is not a separately trained medical model — Anthropic says the feature set 'build[s] on top of major recent improvements we've made to Claude's general intelligence' and named Claude Opus 4.5 as the model backing it at launch; today's live lineup is Claude Opus 5.5 (2026-09-22), Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5, with Claude Fable 5.1 (2026-08-31) as a 'Covered Model' reachable by HIPAA-ready Enterprise and API customers, and Mythos/Opus/Sonnet under the Life Sciences Verification Program for biology-heavy work (2026-09-17). The clinical capability comes from connectors (CMS Coverage Database, ICD-10, NPI Registry, PubMed; HealthEx, Function, Apple Health, Android Health Connect for patients; Medidata, ClinicalTrials.gov, ToolUniverse, bioRxiv/medRxiv, Open Targets, ChEMBL, Owkin, Benchling, 10x Genomics, BioRender, Synapse, Wiley) plus Agent Skills (FHIR development, sample prior-authorization review, clinical-trial protocol drafting) and the anthropics/healthcare plugin with hosted MCP servers (clinical-note-extract, fhir, fraud-detection, icd10-cm, procedure-coding, prior-auth) — i.e. RAG/grounded retrieval over payer and literature databases with citations. Model choice is user-selectable through the Claude model picker and API model IDs; patient health data is explicitly not used for training, but Covered Models (Fable 5/5.1) require 30-day retention so zero-data-retention orgs cannot use them. The most recent healthcare-specific step is athenahealth's athenaPatient MCP (2026-11-02) letting patients query their own records through Claude.

Press at launch described 'models trained specifically for healthcare'; Anthropic's own wording is that it extends general intelligence, so any dedicated medical fine-tune is undisclosed.

tools.modelFamily: Multi-model via Microsoft Azure OpenAI + Epic's proprietary Cosmos foundation models
tools.notes: Epic does not name the LLM behind Art, AI Charting, Emmie, Penny or Agent Factory. Its own public AI page still describes a HIPAA-compliant pipeline that 'incorporates state-of-the-art language models, like GPT-4', and its product timeline records 'Epic supports GPT-4' in 2025. By February 2026 an Epic spokesperson said Epic 'continue[s] to work with Microsoft on AI Charting and use[s] a variety of different models through the Microsoft Azure platform', and Epic's VP of R&D Corey Miller said Epic 'generally uses different models for different specialties and tasks, and accesses those through Microsoft's Azure platform' — so Epic routes across frontier models rather than committing to one, and AI Charting is a separate product from Microsoft's DAX/Dragon. Health systems do get some model selection in Agent Factory: builders pick the model inside the agent portion of a flow, with per-million-token costs passed through. One concrete datapoint from a health-system build-a-thon (WVU Medicine, June 2026): the build environment ran on a single model, OpenAI's ChatGPT 5.1, with others expected to follow. Epic's own foundation model line is Cosmos Curiosity (formerly CoMET), a family of generative medical models trained on 300M+ de-identified Cosmos records that predict future medical events — a medical-event model, not a general-purpose LLM. Epic's AI Charting uses Microsoft Dragon for transcription (on Haiku/Canto devices) but generates notes with its own models.
tools.conflict: Epic's public AI marketing page still cites GPT-4, which is likely stale against a 2026 multi-model Azure stack (GPT-5.1 in an Agent Factory build environment as of June 2026). No Epic source names the model behind any specific shipped feature, so the current model per feature is recorded as undisclosed.
